transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-21
Start: 16:05 PT
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Rita Gomez (Veridian CTO), Samir Patel (Lead Backend Eng), Ellen Wu (ML Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Veridian is evaluating Redwood for a productionized agent orchestration layer that heavily uses function/tool calling and structured JSON outputs. Primary concerns: end-to-end latency for short-turn interactions, correctness of structured outputs, ability to run within Veridian VPC for regulated datasets, and predictable unit economics. Action items: share benchmark harness, sample traffic, security docs; align on success criteria and acceptance tests.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um I think we have about 50 minutes, so we'll run through scope and then nail down next steps. Ethan, you wanna quick intro?
[00:18] Ethan: yeah sure, hey Rita, Samir, Ellen, i'm ethan, i'm a solutions engineer at Redwood, focus on integrations and benchmarking, we'll talk through how to set up an OpenAI-compatible endpoint and the function-calling flow you mentioned. small note: some of my slides use older product names so ignore if it says 'Redwood Dedicated' it's the same idea.
[00:37] Rita: great, thank you. high level — our use case is a conversational routing agent that calls internal services (inventory, billing, customer profile). We need structured JSON responses for downstream systems and the ability to call tools with tokens masked for privacy.
[00:55] Samir: and from infra, our constraints: typical traffic is bursted, peak 120 rps for 2 minute windows, steady 6 rps baseline. average prompt sizes are around 1.2k tokens, sometimes up to 3k for long customer histories.
[01:18] Ellen: also note we plan to run initial POC in a VPC-connected private deployment due to data residency, then consider hosted if SLA and contract allow.
[01:35] Ethan: got it. couple of clarifying qs: success criteria — do you want target latency P95, max cost per 1M tokens, or a combination? and how important is model parity with your current OpenAI baseline?
[01:52] Rita: combination — P95 latency under 500ms for short prompts (<=512 tokens) is ideal, but we'll accept up to 800ms for longer ones; cost goals are 30% below our current hosted bill at scale, accuracy / structured output fidelity has to match or exceed current rules-based extraction.
[02:15] Maya: quick note, our OpenAI-compatible endpoints support the same request/response schema including function calling and streaming, so your SDKs should map with minimal changes. there are caveats around version pinning for models and quantization impacts on small token latencies.
[02:36] Samir: can you explain quantization impacts? last time we tried a 4-bit quantized model it saved cost but p95 latency got worse on some sequence lengths.
[02:51] Ethan: yeah, quantization reduces memory and compute, but kernel selection and attention algorithm differs; for short sequences the overhead of some quantized kernels can add a millisecond or two per token. For your target 500ms P95 on <=512 tokens we recommend trying a bf16 / q8 variant in the first run, then compare cost/latency tradeoffs.
[03:17] Rita: timeline wise we want a 3-week POC: week 1 integration + traffic provisioning, week 2 benchmarking + tune, week 3 acceptance and decision. Is that feasible?
[03:33] Ethan: feasible if we get sample traces this week and can spin up a dedicated trial pool or a VPC deployment. For dedicated capacity there's a small lead time; private VPC trial we can run a short-lived instance within 48–72 hours if networking is ready.
[03:51] Maya: also we'll need an SSO admin to approve service account and RBAC; Samir, who owns that on your side?
[03:59] Samir: that's me, i'll coordinate. we'll need an IP allowlist for the trial and a temporary KMS key to test envelope encryption — Ellen, you good to handle that?
[04:10] Ellen: yep, i'll work on KMS and we have a managed HSM via our cloud provider, we can provide wrapped keys, though we'll need instructions for Redwood's key import flow.
[04:25] Ethan: note: our private deployment supports both bring-your-own-KMS and Redwood-managed KMS; for the trial BYO is preferred to validate key rotation. we'll drop a KMS integration guide.
[04:40] [crosstalk] Rita: okay excellent.
[04:45] Ethan: on benchmarks — our recommended harness runs three workload profiles:
[04:52] Ethan: 1) short-turn interactive (<=256 tokens) — latency-focused, 200 concurrent connections, 100 rps sustained for 10 minutes;
[05:02] Ethan: 2) mid-turn contextual (512-1.5k tokens) — mixed latency/throughput, 50 rps bursts;
[05:08] Ethan: 3) long-history retrieval (2k-4k tokens) — throughput focused, lower qps but high token counts.
[05:20] Samir: that aligns with our patterns. how do you measure structured output correctness? we need exact JSON keys and valid schemas — no soft-parsing.
[05:31] Ethan: we include schema-validation steps: the harness submits golden prompts and checks model outputs against JSON schema using strict validation (fail on missing/extra keys). we also track semantic fidelity with a small eval set using your production labels.
[05:46] Rita: perfect. what's the SLA for model rollout if we want to pin a version? we need predictable behavior across rollouts.
[05:55] Maya: you can pin exact model versions and rollout policies; we support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a safe variant if quality drops. we'll also retain per-route logs for audits.
[06:07] Samir: logging/audit question — we need full request/response logs for debugging but cannot store PII. can we redact or mask tokens in logs?
[06:16] Ethan: yes, we can implement token redaction at ingest and also provide token-level cost accounting without exposing raw PII. for the POC we'll show redaction configs and a sample redacted log set.
[06:30] Ellen: on SDKs: our stack uses server-side Node.js microservices. we currently call OpenAI endpoints through a thin adapter. is migrating to Redwood as simple as swapping endpoints?
[06:40] Ethan: in most cases yes — our OpenAI-compatible endpoint matches request shapes (function calling, messages, streaming). if you use advanced features (prefix caching, custom KV cache), you'll add a small client-side library. we also have a node SDK with retry/backoff that mirrors openai-js semantics.
[06:58] Maya: quick gotcha — streaming with function calling has a few edge cases: sometimes function arguments arrive across multiple chunks; the SDK buffers and assembles, but integration tests must include chunked streaming.
[07:12] Rita: good to know. for acceptance tests, we want: automated schema validation, P95 latency targets at short/mid profiles, throughput checks for long history flows, and an economic projection (cost per M tokens vs current).
[07:29] Ethan: we'll include those metrics in the harness and produce a report with token-level cost breakdown, latency histograms, and failure modes.
[07:40] Samir: what's your recommended concurrency model for our peak bursts? we have those 2-minute 120 rps spikes.
[07:48] Ethan: continuous batching helps, but bursts require autoscale headroom. For private VPC trials, we recommend a reserve pool sized for 150 rps to avoid cold starts. For hosted API, we route across regions and fallback tiers.
[08:02] Maya: also there's a configuration knob — max inflight tokens per worker — which you can tune to prioritize latency vs throughput.
[08:12] Ellen: about function/tool calling — we will call internal services that require auth headers and idempotency. can the function call payloads include opaque service tokens?
[08:23] Ethan: yes, function call payloads can contain opaque tokens; we recommend never persisting them in logs and using short-lived tokens. for the POC we'll show a pattern using session-scoped tokens + signed request wrapper.
[08:40] Rita: do you support structured output best-effort plus deterministic fallback? e.g., if model fails schema, fall back to a templated extractor.
[08:48] Ethan: yes, that's a common pattern: primary model with schema enforcement, automatic retry with a different model variant, or fallback to a deterministic extractor. we can codify policies in the route config.
[09:02] Samir: on metrics, do you expose per-route P95 and per-customer billing? we need both for chargeback.
[09:11] Maya: yes, per-route telemetry and token-level chargeback is available; we can map to your internal project IDs.
[09:19] Ellen: security review question — SOC2 and ISO paperwork, plus penetration test reports, do you provide those before a private deployment?
[09:29] Maya: we can provide SOC2 Type II, ISO cert summary, and a red-team exec summary; full pentest reports are shared under NDA. we'll include the doc pack in the next email.
[09:42] Rita: perfect. concerning failure modes — if a canary fails schema checks, how is the traffic diverted?
[09:50] Ethan: built-in rollout policy can automatically divert all traffic to previous stable model or route to hosted fallback region. your choice.
[09:58] Samir: about cost projections — can you run a side-by-side cost sim given our sample traces?
[10:05] Ethan: yep, that's part of the benchmark deliverable: we run your traces against our cost model (tokens, compute, cache hits) and output a per-month projection at scale.
[10:16] Rita: do you support function-calling chains? our orchestration sometimes calls 3 services sequentially in one user turn.
[10:25] Ethan: support for multi-step function chains exists; we recommend short-circuit caching for repeated calls and also turning on idempotency keys. watch for KV cache growth across chained calls.
[10:40] [pause / typing sounds]
[10:50] Maya: on timelines — confirm the 3-week POC; we need to lock resources. i'll send a proposed calendar invite with milestones after this call.
[11:00] Samir: one more infra nuance: our egress policies limit outbound IP ranges; what exactly will you need?
[11:08] Ethan: for the VPC trial you'll provide an allowlist and we'll supply the minimal set of IPs for the trial and CIDs for our control plane. for dedicated/private we can also do peering.
[11:20] Ellen: will there be any changes needed to our model-adapter logic besides endpoint swap? we have custom parsing today.
[11:28] Ethan: likely minor: update streaming assembly and error codes mapping; we'll share a migration shim that is just a handful lines.
[11:38] Rita: ok, let's recap success criteria aloud: 1) schema pass rate >= 99% on golden set, 2) P95 <= 500ms for <=512 tokens, 3) cost projection 30% below baseline at target scale, 4) private deployment with BYO-KMS for trial. anything to add?
[11:58] Maya: add retention & audit: ability to configure retention windows and redaction for PII.
[12:06] Rita: agreed.
[12:09] Ethan: i'll draft the benchmark plan and share the harness repo. also we'll include a short sample of streaming + function-calling chunked payloads so you can run integration tests locally.
[12:21] Maya: i'll put together the security pack and pricing, and send calendar for kickoff.
[12:26] Samir: i'll get logs and token distributions to you by Wednesday. Ellen will handle the KMS key exchange instructions.
[12:36] Rita: thanks everyone — sounds good.
[12:40] Maya: great, we'll follow up with action items and timeline. thanks all.

End meeting.
